United States.text:
As World Cup hosts, the United States get a kind start: the model has them through the group stage 87.1% of the time, top of the group at 47.7%, and into the round of 16 at 56.2%. Beyond that the picture narrows fast — a 26.9% quarter-final chance, 10.7% to reach the semis, and just 1.7% to lift the trophy on home soil. Ranked 16th by FIFA with a squad valued at €385.65m, this is a competitive side rather than a favourite, and the numbers treat the latter rounds as a steep climb.

The form line is the worry. Across their last ten, the USMNT beat Uruguay 5-1, Paraguay, Australia and Japan, but also lost 2-5 to Belgium, 0-2 to Portugal and, most recently, 1-2 at home to Germany in June. The pattern is plain: they handle teams around or below their level and get punished by the elite. A friendly schedule stacked with European heavyweights has exposed that gap, and how they fare in the knockouts will hinge on whether they can finally close it against a top-tier opponent.

Canada.text:
As one of the host nations, Canada arrives ranked 30th in the world with a squad valued at €198.65m, and the model treats them as comfortable favourites to escape the group stage — a 97.8% chance of reaching the round of 32 and 63.1% to make the round of 16. The harder questions come later: a quarter-final is roughly a one-in-four shot at 27.0%, a semi-final drops to 8.7%, and the title is priced as a long shot at 0.85%. Home advantage and a deep, organised defensive group anchored by Crépeau in goal and Johnston and Laryea behind it underpin that floor.

The form line is steady rather than spectacular. Across their last ten, all but one at home, Canada won four, drew five and lost only once, that single defeat coming against Australia. The recent friendlies tell a story of solidity over firepower — 0-0 draws with Colombia, Ecuador and Tunisia, plus the 1-1 with the Republic of Ireland in June. That tightness explains the strong group-win number of 56.8%, but the shortage of goals is why the model cools sharply once the knockouts arrive.

Mexico.text:
As hosts, Mexico arrive in form. The last competitive defeat on record is the 1-2 loss to Paraguay in November 2025; since then they have gone nine matches unbeaten, including goalless draws with Portugal and Uruguay and emphatic friendly wins over Iceland (4-0) and Serbia (5-1). That run, married to home advantage and a FIFA ranking of 15, is why the model makes them clear favourites to top their group at 58 percent and gives them a 56.9 percent chance of reaching the round of 16. The squad is valued at €191.85m, modest by the standards of the genuine contenders.

That last point is the honest caveat. Beyond the last 16 the numbers thin out quickly: a 24 percent shot at the quarter-finals, 8 percent at the semis, and just 0.83 percent to lift the trophy. So the realistic ceiling here is a deep-ish run rather than a title challenge, and the friendly form, however tidy, came against a mixed bag of opposition with several 1-0 results. Treat the group-stage optimism as well founded and the knockout maths as the sterner test.

Panama.text:
Panama arrive ranked 33rd in the world, a CONCACAF side carrying one of the lighter squads in the field at €34.55m, and the model treats them accordingly. It gives them just a 28.1% chance of escaping the group into the round of 32, 3.8% to reach the round of 16, and effectively nothing beyond — 0.5% to the quarter-finals, and no realistic path to a final. Winning the group, at 1.66%, is close to a non-event. This is a team the numbers expect to compete for survival rather than progression.

The recent form reads as genuinely split. Qualifying went well — a 3-0 win over El Salvador, a 3-2 win in Guatemala, a draw with Suriname — but the friendlies since have been uneven: a 4-2 win over the Dominican Republic and a 2-1 win in South Africa sit alongside a 2-6 hammering by Brazil, a 1-1 draw with Bosnia and a 0-1 home loss to Mexico. The ceiling against weaker opposition is real; the floor against elite sides is just as real, and the 28.1% R32 figure splits that difference honestly.

Argentina.text:
Argentina arrive as the defending champions and the model treats them like it: an 18.8% shot at lifting the trophy again, the kind of number that puts them among the very short list of genuine contenders. Ranked third by FIFA and carrying a squad valued at €782.5m, la Albiceleste look the part. The recent form backs it up — they've won nine of their last ten, including a 6-0 dismantling of Puerto Rico and a 5-0 win over Zambia, with the only blemish a 0-1 defeat away to Ecuador in qualifying last September.

The model gives them a 76% chance of topping their group and rates them clear favourites to reach the last 16 at 71.3%, but the path narrows fast after that: 58.4% to make the quarter-finals, 43.2% for the semis, and just 28.5% to reach the final. That drop is the honest reality of knockout football — even an elite side faces compounding coin-flips against fellow heavyweights. The headline 18.8% title figure leaves Argentina firmly in the conversation without crowning them, which feels about right for a champion that still has to prove it twice over.

Brazil.text:
Brazil arrive ranked sixth in the world and carrying a squad valued at €928.2m, and the model treats them as genuine contenders rather than outright favourites: a 10.2% shot at the title, 17.9% to reach the final, and a 61.6% chance of topping their group. The path is friendly early — reaching the round of 32 is close to a formality at 98.2% — but the numbers cool quickly thereafter, with the round of 16 at 68.7% and the quarter-final a near coin-flip at 48.6%. This is a team the model expects to go deep without banking on a coronation.

The recent form tells you why the projection stops short of certainty. The pre-tournament run looks strong on paper — wins over Egypt, Panama, Croatia, Senegal and South Korea, plus a 3-0 qualifying win over Chile — but mixed in are a home defeat to France, a draw with Tunisia, and losses to Japan and, strikingly, Bolivia away in qualifying. With Alisson, Ederson and a backline built around Gabriel Magalhães and Bremer, the talent is unquestioned; the consistency, on this evidence, is the open question.

Colombia.text:
Los Cafeteros arrive ranked 13th in the world and carrying a €302m squad, and their recent form reads like a team peaking at the right time. The two June friendlies — a 2-0 win over Jordan and a 3-1 dismantling of Costa Rica — followed eye-catching results in qualifying, including a 6-3 thrashing of Venezuela and a 3-0 win over Bolivia. The blemishes are honest ones: back-to-back home losses to Croatia (1-2) and France (1-3) in March suggest the gap to Europe's elite is real, even if the wider body of work is strong.

The model likes them without loving them. Colombia are given a 34.8% chance to win their group and an 86.8% shot at surviving to the round of 32, but the odds thin quickly thereafter — 56.4% to reach the last 16, 29.9% to make the quarters, and just 6.8% to reach the final. The 2.9% title number frames the ceiling plainly: this is a side good enough to trouble anyone on its day, yet not one the numbers expect to go all the way. A deep run is plausible; a coronation would be a surprise.

Uruguay.text:
Marcelo Bielsa's Uruguay arrive ranked 17th in the world and carrying a squad worth €359.3m, but recent form muddies the picture. The qualifying body of work was solid enough — a 3-0 win over Peru, 2-0 over Venezuela, a goalless draw in Chile — yet the friendly run since has been uneven. Creditable away draws against England (1-1) and Algeria (0-0) sit beside a chastening 1-5 defeat in the USA and a blank against Mexico. For a side built around defenders like Araújo and Giménez, the leaking of five goals in a single night is the kind of result that lingers.

The model treats them as a strong but not elite outfit. Reaching the round of 32 is close to a formality at 90.6%, and there's a 37.2% chance of surviving to the last 16, but the odds thin quickly after that: 21.2% to reach the quarters, 10.8% the semis, and just 1.9% to lift the trophy. Winning their group is rated only 22.6%, so a tougher knockout path looks the likelier route — and on that road, the back line's recent wobbles matter.

Ecuador.text:
Ecuador arrive unbeaten across their last ten, a run that says less about firepower than about how hard they are to break down: four wins and six draws, with 0-0s against Paraguay and Canada, 1-1 stalemates with the Netherlands and Morocco, and a 1-0 home win over Argentina in qualifying. That defensive backbone is where the €368.7m squad value concentrates, in names like Pacho, Hincapié, Ordoñez and Estupiñán. The recent friendly wins over Guatemala (3-0) and Saudi Arabia (2-1) hint at a sharper edge, but the pattern of low-scoring draws is the truer signal for a side ranked 23rd in the world.

The model treats them as a solid knockout team rather than a contender. It gives La Tricolor an 89.6% chance of clearing the group stage and 48.9% of reaching the last 16, essentially a coin flip, before the odds thin to 21.6% for the quarters and just 1.5% to lift the trophy. Winning their group sits at 28.2%, so a runners-up route looks the likelier path. Grind out results, and the round of 16 is genuinely within reach.

Paraguay.text:
Paraguay arrive ranked 40th in the world, a side whose pedigree — ten World Cup appearances, a quarter-final in 2010 and two Copa América titles — outstrips a fairly modest squad value of €153.65m. The form is genuinely mixed. La Albirroja closed their South American qualifying campaign solidly enough, a 1-0 win in Peru and a goalless draw at home to Ecuador either side of a narrow loss in Brazil, but the friendly run since has wobbled, with defeats to the USA, South Korea and Morocco offset by wins over Mexico and Greece and a thumping 4-0 over Nicaragua in June. The defence, built around Alderete, Balbuena and Gómez, is the recognisable backbone.

The model treats them as a side likely to survive but unlikely to surge. It gives Paraguay a 52.9% chance of getting out of the expanded group stage but only 11.98% to win the group outright, and the odds thin sharply from there: 20.7% to reach the last 16, 5.6% to the quarter-finals, and just 0.08% to lift the trophy. A team to respect defensively, not one the numbers expect to run deep.

Germany.text:
Germany arrive in form. Nine wins from their last ten leaves only a 0-2 defeat at Slovakia in September 2025 as a blemish, and they avenged it emphatically with a 6-0 thrashing in November. The qualifying run was ruthless — four clean sheets, double-digit goals across the Luxembourg and Northern Ireland fixtures — and the friendlies kept the momentum going, with a 4-0 dismissal of Finland and a 2-1 win away to the USA in early June. Ranked tenth by FIFA and carrying a squad valued at €947m, this is a side built to go deep.

The model, though, is more measured than the results sheet suggests. Germany are near-certain to clear the group stage at 96.2%, but only 48.9% to actually win their group, and the odds thin quickly after that: 30.2% to reach the quarter-finals, 15.2% for the semis, and just 2.8% to lift the trophy. That gap between glittering form and a cautious title number is the honest tension here — a team good enough to beat anyone on the day, but not yet priced as a favourite to win seven straight.

England.text:
England arrive ranked fourth in the world with a squad valued at €1.36bn, and the qualifying campaign backed that billing up: five straight European wins, Serbia beaten 5-0 away and 2-0 at home, Latvia thumped 5-0, and not a goal conceded across the run. The model likes them accordingly, making England 74.1% to win their group and the near-certainty of 98.6% to clear the round of 32. That is the profile of a side expected to be there in the closing stages.

The warm-up form complicates the picture. Since qualifying wrapped up England have lost 0-1 to Japan and drawn 1-1 with Uruguay at home before scraping past New Zealand 1-0, and a 1-3 friendly loss to Senegal lingers from June. So the deep-run numbers come with caveats: the model gives 50.7% to reach the quarter-finals, 31.0% the semis, but only 17.8% to make the final and 10.3% to lift the trophy. Strong enough to be among the favourites, not strong enough to be trusted blindly — the friendly stumbles are a genuine question the knockouts will answer.

France.text:
France arrive as the world's number one ranked side and the most valuable squad in the field at €1.52bn, and the form backs the billing: eight wins in their last ten, including away victories over Brazil and Colombia in March and a flawless run through European qualifying bar a 2-2 draw in Iceland. The two blemishes are recent, a 1-2 home loss to Ivory Coast in June being the one result that interrupts an otherwise commanding stretch for Les Bleus. With Maignan behind a defence stacked with the Hernández brothers and Konaté, the spine looks as strong as anyone's.

The model makes France genuine contenders without quite installing them as favourites. It gives them a 55.9% chance of winning their group and 95.8% to clear the round of 32, but the odds thin as the bracket does: 46% to reach the quarter-finals, 28.1% the semis, and 15.5% to make the final. The bottom line is an 8.1% title probability, meaning the model has France lifting the trophy roughly one tournament in twelve, the favourite tag they carry on paper notwithstanding.

Spain.text:
Ranked second in the world and carrying a squad valued at €1.22bn, Spain arrive as one of the genuine contenders, and the model agrees: a 14.2% title chance is among the shortest in the field, with a 24.2% shot at reaching the final and a 50.4% chance of seeing out the quarter-finals. Winning their group is treated as the likely outcome at 74.8%, and survival to the last 32 is all but assumed at 99.2%. This is the profile of a team expected to go deep rather than merely turn up.

The form behind those numbers is split. European qualifying was emphatic — six wins including 6-0 away to Türkiye, 4-0 against both Georgia and Bulgaria, before a 2-2 home draw with Türkiye took the gloss off. The spring and summer friendlies have been flatter still: a goalless draw with Egypt and a 1-1 against Iraq sit awkwardly beside the 3-1 win over Peru and 3-0 over Serbia. The model still rates them a championship-class side, but the recent stutters are a fair reason to keep that 14.2% honest rather than treat the title as anything close to settled.

Portugal.text:
Roberto Martínez's Portugal arrive ranked fifth in the world with a squad valued at just over a billion euros, and the model treats them as serious contenders without quite installing them as favourites: a 6.8% chance of lifting the trophy, 13% of reaching the final, and a 53.6% shot at topping their group. Survival to the knockouts looks close to a formality at 93.2% to clear the round of 32, though the path narrows quickly — 69.2% to reach the last 16, then 44.1% into the quarter-finals.

The form line is mostly reassuring rather than dominant. They closed qualifying with a 9-1 demolition of Armenia and beat Hungary home and away, but a 0-2 loss in Ireland and a 2-2 home draw with Hungary are reminders that this side can be got at. Recent friendlies — wins over Chile and the USA either side of a goalless draw in Mexico — fit the same pattern of comfortable but not ruthless. With Rúben Dias and Diogo Costa anchoring a strong defensive spine, Portugal have the squad to go deep; the model's caution suggests the difference between contender and champion still hangs on the margins.

Netherlands.text:
The Netherlands arrive seventh in the world and carrying a €754.2m squad built on a familiar defensive spine — Van Dijk, Aké, Dumfries and Timber in front of a three-man goalkeeping rotation of Flekken, Roefs and Verbruggen. Their qualifying campaign did the job without ever looking imperious: four 4-0 wins over Lithuania, Finland and Malta sat alongside two 1-1 draws with Poland, the kind of record that gets you to a World Cup but leaves questions about the very top end.

The model reads them as a solid second-tier contender rather than a favourite. It gives them a 90.1% chance of clearing the opening round and a 43.1% shot at winning their group, but the odds thin quickly after that — 42.0% to reach the last 16, 25.2% to make the quarters, and just 2.4% to lift the trophy. Recent friendlies offer little reassurance: a 0-1 home loss to Algeria and a 1-1 draw with Ecuador in spring, sandwiching narrow wins over Uzbekistan and Norway. The pieces are clearly there; the form, for now, is asking to be convinced.

Belgium.text:
Belgium arrive ranked ninth in the world and carrying the form to match: their last ten games include a 5-0 demolition of Tunisia, a 2-0 win away to Croatia and a string of heavy qualifying victories, among them 7-0 over Liechtenstein and 6-0 against Kazakhstan. The blemishes are the draws — 1-1 in Kazakhstan, 0-0 at home to FYR Macedonia and 1-1 in Mexico — which suggest a side that crushes weaker opponents but can be frustrated by organised ones. With a squad valued at €547.5m and Thibaut Courtois behind a back line built around Castagne, Debast and Mechele, the platform is there.

The model makes them clear favourites to win their group at 63 percent, and reaching the last 32 is close to a formality at 94 percent. Beyond that the path narrows quickly: a 66 percent shot at the round of 16, but only 36 percent to reach the quarter-finals and 16 percent to make the semis. The title number is a sober 2.9 percent — Belgium look a safe bet to advance, but not yet a credible one to lift the trophy.

Austria.text:
Austria arrive at the World Cup ranked 24th in the world and carrying a tidy run of results: three straight friendly wins in 2026, including a 5-1 dismantling of Ghana, on top of a qualifying campaign that featured a 10-0 thrashing of San Marino and a 2-1 win away in Bosnia. The only real blemishes were a 1-0 loss in Romania and a home draw with Bosnia, so the recent body of work points to a side that wins the matches it should and rarely embarrasses itself.

The model is more measured. It gives Austria a 71% chance of clearing the group stage and reaching the round of 32, but only 21% to make the round of 16 and 8.3% to reach the quarter-finals. Winning the group sits at a modest 8%, and a deep run is treated as a long shot — 2.5% to reach the semis, just 0.17% to lift the trophy. With a squad valued at €242.2m and experience like David Alaba at the back, this is a team built to compete and advance, but the numbers frame anything beyond the last 16 as genuine overachievement.

Switzerland.text:
Switzerland arrive 19th in the world and in the kind of form that qualifying campaigns are built on: across their last six European qualifiers they dropped points only in goalless draws away to Slovenia and Kosovo, while putting four past both Sweden and Kosovo at home and winning in Sweden 2-0. The friendlies since have been scruffier — a 4-3 home loss to Germany, a 1-1 draw with Australia — but a 4-1 win over Jordan and a £332.5m squad anchored by Manchester City's Manuel Akanji suggest a side that knows what it is.

The model treats them as a solid second seed rather than a contender. Reaching the round of 32 is close to a formality at 95.5%, and they are roughly even money to clear the round of 16 at 55.4%, but winning the group is only a 39.6% shot and the quarter-finals already thin out to 20.2%. Beyond that the numbers fall away fast — 6.9% to make a semi-final, 0.7% to lift the trophy. This is a team built to advance steadily and then run into someone better; the open question is simply how deep the steady stretch runs.

Turkey.text:
Turkey arrive in good form, winning eight of their last ten and going unbeaten across their final stretch of European qualifying, including a 2-2 draw away to Spain in November. The blot on that record is glaring, though: a 0-6 home defeat to the same Spain side in September, the kind of result that shows how quickly things can unravel against elite opposition. Ranked 22nd in the world with a squad valued at €473.7m, this is a team that brushes aside the likes of Bulgaria 6-1 and Georgia 4-1, but the gap to the top tier remains real.

The model sees Turkey as solid rather than special. They are roughly a coin-flip to win their group at 19.3%, with a 64.7% chance of clearing the round of 32 and a 30.0% shot at reaching the last 16. Beyond that the numbers thin out fast: 9.4% to make the quarter-finals, 2.7% for the semis, and just 0.17% to lift the trophy. That feels about right for a side capable of beating anyone on its day and losing heavily on its worst.

Croatia.text:
Croatia arrive ranked 11th in the world and reached the 2026 finals on the back of a tidy European qualifying campaign: six wins and a goalless draw away in the Czech Republic, with a 4-0 thrashing of Montenegro and a 3-0 of Gibraltar showing they can pile on goals when invited to. The warm-up form has been choppier, though. A 2-1 home win over Slovenia on 7 June steadied things, but it came after a 0-2 home defeat to Belgium and a 1-3 loss in Brazil — a reminder that the step up against serious opposition still bites. The squad, valued at €387.3m and built around Gvardiol at the back, is experienced rather than overwhelming.

The model reads them as solid but not elite. Reaching the round of 32 is close to a formality at 86.9%, and they win their group only about a fifth of the time (20.5%). From there the probabilities thin quickly: 38.4% to reach the last 16, 14.4% to the quarter-finals, and just 5.8% to lift the trophy. A deep run is plausible; a coronation is not what the numbers expect.

Scotland.text:
Scotland arrive ranked 43rd in the world, and they got here the hard way: a qualifying campaign that delivered a 0-0 draw in Denmark, then a 4-2 win over the same Danes at Hampden in November, with home and away results against Greece going one apiece. The warm-up form reads oddly — 0-1 losses to Japan and Ivory Coast in March, then emphatic 4-1 and 4-0 friendly wins over Curaçao and Bolivia in late spring. A squad valued at €170.25m and built around experienced goalkeepers and defenders looks organised rather than star-laden.

The model treats this as a tournament about survival, not silverware. It gives Scotland a 42.8% chance of clearing the round of 32 but only 10.6% to reach the last 16, and the numbers fall off a cliff beyond that — 2.5% to the quarter-finals, 0.5% to a semi, and essentially nothing, 0.02%, to lift the trophy. Winning the group sits at just 2.8%. The honest read: getting out of the group stage is the realistic target, and even that is closer to a coin-flip than a formality.

Morocco.text:
Morocco arrive ranked eighth in the world and in the form of their lives. The Atlas Lions are unbeaten across their last ten, a run that includes a clean march through the Africa Cup of Nations — 3-0 at Zambia, then wins over Tanzania, Cameroon and Nigeria before a 3-0 dismantling of Senegal away. Recent friendlies have been similarly emphatic, 5-0 against Burundi and 4-0 against Madagascar, with only draws against Norway and Ecuador to interrupt the wins. A squad valued at €498.3m, anchored by Bounou in goal and Hakimi and Aguerd at the back, is built to defend leads and grind out results.

The model likes them, though not as outright contenders. It gives Morocco a 94.3% chance of clearing the group stage and a 34.3% shot at topping the group, but the odds thin quickly thereafter: 56.5% to reach the last 16, 36.1% to make the quarter-finals, and just 4.7% to lift the trophy. That makes them a credible dark horse rather than a favourite — a side most opponents will badly want to avoid.

Senegal.text:
Senegal arrive ranked 14th in the world with a squad valued at €478.1m, and the model treats them as a solid knockout side rather than a contender: 83.4% to clear the group stage and 46.75% to reach the last 16, but only 21.5% to make the quarter-finals and 1.4% to lift the trophy. Winning their group is rated a 22.6% shot, so the projection sees them advancing more often than not while rarely going deep. The depth at goalkeeper alone — Mendy, Diaw and Diouf — and a backline featuring Koulibaly and Niakhaté underpin a profile built on defensive solidity.

The recent form is a mixed read. The Africa Cup of Nations run was strong, with five wins including 1-0 results over Mali and Egypt, before a 0-3 collapse against Morocco ended it bluntly. Since then the friendlies have been uneven: a 2-0 win over Peru and a 3-1 win over Gambia, but a 2-3 loss to the USA in late May. The numbers say a team that should reach the knockouts comfortably, with the open question being how far the defence can carry them.

Egypt.text:
Ranked 29th in the world with a squad valued at €116.48m, Egypt arrive carrying the familiar shape of a side that defends well and scores in small margins. The recent form reads as a team in transition: a tidy 1-0 friendly win over Russia in May, a goalless draw away to Spain in March and a 4-0 dismantling of Saudi Arabia point to genuine ceiling, but the Africa Cup of Nations told a harder story, with the run ending in defeats to Senegal and Nigeria after early wins over Benin and Ivory Coast. The Pharaohs were beaten 1-2 by Brazil in their last outing.

The model treats them as solid but not dangerous. It gives Egypt a 68.1% chance of clearing the group stage and reaching the round of 32, but only 27.3% to make the last 16 and 15.4% to actually win their group. Beyond that the numbers thin out fast — 7.5% to reach the quarter-finals, 2% a semi-final, and just a 0.1% shot at the title. This is a team built to survive the opening hurdle, with everything after that an uphill climb.

Ivory Coast.text:
The Elephants arrive in good order. The reigning African champions — their third continental title came in 2023 — have been busy beating proper opposition, edging France 2-1 and Scotland 1-0 away, and thumping South Korea 4-0, all on the road. Ranked 34th by FIFA and carrying a squad worth €522.1m, this is a side built on defensive talent, with Kossounou, Diomande and Agbadou anchoring a back line and three goalkeepers in Fofana, Koné and Lafont fighting for the gloves.

The model likes them to advance but not much more. It gives Ivory Coast an 85.8% chance of clearing the round of 32 and a 41.6% shot at the last 16, but only a 22.3% chance of actually winning their group — a coin-toss-and-then-some that frames the opening matches as the real test. Beyond that the numbers thin out fast: 16.2% to reach the quarter-finals, 6.2% to the semis, and just 0.71% to lift the trophy. A strong recent run and a settled defence make the knockout rounds a realistic target; the deeper stages remain a long shot.

South Africa.text:
Bafana Bafana arrive at the World Cup ranked 60th in the world and carrying one of the lighter squads in the field, valued at just €49.25m. The model treats them as long-odds participants: a 33.8% chance of reaching the round of 32 and only 7.2% to advance to the round of 16, with winning the group rated at 4.3% and a quarter-final at barely 1%. Those are the numbers of a side expected to make up the bracket rather than disturb it, and recent form does little to argue otherwise — South Africa have not won in their last four, drawing 1-1 with Jamaica, 0-0 with Nicaragua and splitting two meetings with Panama either side of a March defeat.

Their Africa Cup of Nations campaign offered the same mixed picture: wins over Angola and Zimbabwe sat beside losses to Egypt and Cameroon. With a goalkeeper-and-defender-heavy key cohort and none of the listed names carrying recorded international goals, the attacking question is real. The model's verdict is honest rather than harsh — a team capable of nicking a result, but short of the firepower a deep run demands.

DR Congo.text:
The Leopards arrive ranked 46th in the world, with a squad valued at €143.9m and a recent run that suggests genuine momentum. They beat Cameroon 1-0 away and took a result off Nigeria away in November qualifying, then edged Jamaica 1-0 in the intercontinental play-off to book their place. At the Africa Cup of Nations they beat Benin and Botswana and drew with Senegal before a narrow 0-1 loss to Algeria, and a 0-0 friendly draw with Denmark in June shows they can hold their shape against quality. That backbone runs through experienced defenders like Kalulu, Masuaku and Batubinsika in front of competing goalkeepers Epolo, Fayulu and Mpasi.

The model is more measured. It gives DR Congo a 41.1% chance of surviving the group into the round of 32, but only 12.4% to reach the last 16 and 3.3% to make a quarter-final. Winning the group is a long shot at 5.4%, and a title run sits at 0.03% — effectively a rounding error. The honest read: a side capable of upsets and grinding out clean sheets, but one the numbers expect to bow out early.

Tunisia.text:
The Eagles of Carthage arrive ranked 44th in the world, one of seven World Cup appearances in their history, but the form line heading in is a worry. Their two final warm-ups brought a 0-1 defeat in Austria and a 0-5 thrashing in Belgium, and across the last four friendlies Tunisia have managed a single goal — a 1-0 win over Haiti — alongside a goalless draw with Canada. The Africa Cup of Nations earlier in the season was equally uneven: a 3-1 win over Uganda, but a 3-2 loss to Nigeria and draws with Tanzania and Mali that left little momentum.

The model treats them as outsiders, and the numbers back that up. A €69.95m squad is among the lighter at the tournament, and Tunisia are given just a 5.25% chance of winning their group and a 39.1% shot at surviving to the round of 32. Beyond that the path narrows fast — 8.9% to reach the last 16, 2.45% to the quarter-finals. On recent evidence, finding goals will decide whether they outrun those odds.

Japan.text:
Japan arrive in form that demands attention: their last ten reads like a statement, with 1-0 away wins over England and Scotland in March, a 3-0 dismissal of Bolivia, and a 3-2 friendly defeat of Brazil last October. The blemishes are minor and old — a 0-2 loss in the USA and a goalless draw in Mexico back in September — and the recent run of three straight 1-0 wins points to a side that defends a lead well. Ranked 18th in the world, with a squad valued at €270.85m, this is a tournament-hardened group built around defenders like Itakura, Ito and the veteran Nagatomo.

The model likes them to advance but stops short of treating them as contenders. It gives Japan a 43.4% chance to win their group and a 90.2% chance to reach the round of 32, but the path narrows quickly: 43.1% to make the last 16, 26.5% to reach the quarter-finals, and just 2.8% to lift the trophy. That is the profile of a solid, well-organised side likely to escape its group, with the deeper knockout rounds a genuine open question rather than an expectation.

South Korea.text:
South Korea arrive ranked 25th in the world and valued at a modest €139.05m, and the model treats them as a side that should advance but won't go deep. The expanded format makes the group stage comfortable on paper: an 80.9% chance of reaching the round of 32 and a 25.9% shot at winning the group. After that the numbers thin out fast, with 36.7% to reach the last 16, 11.2% for the quarter-finals and just 0.2% to lift the trophy. This is a team the model expects to survive the opening hurdle and then meet its ceiling.

The form line explains the caution. Korea closed their build-up with confident home wins, 1-0 over El Salvador and 5-0 against Trinidad and Tobago, and earlier away results at the USA (2-0) and Mexico (2-2) read well. But the same stretch contains heavy defeats — 0-5 to Brazil, 0-4 to Ivory Coast and 0-1 in Austria — that show how quickly things unravel against stronger opposition. With a strong goalkeeping pool and Kim Min-Jae anchoring the back line, the floor is solid; it's the ceiling against elite sides that the results question.

Iran.text:
Iran arrive ranked 21st in the world and in decent touch, with three friendly wins on the spin including a 5-0 thumping of Costa Rica away and a 2-0 home win over Mali in June. The deeper run, though, was choppier: defeats to Russia and Nigeria, a 1-2 loss to Uzbekistan at home in the CAFA Nations Cup and a draw with Tajikistan suggest a side that can carve up modest opposition but stalls against organised, motivated teams. The squad is goalkeeper-heavy on paper — Beiranvand, Hosseini and Niazmand all listed — and valued at just €32.05m, modest for this stage.

The model reads them as a team built to survive rather than surge. It gives Iran a 66.7% chance of clearing the group into the round of 32, but only 25.7% to reach the last 16 and 6.8% to make a quarter-final. Winning the group is priced at 15.3%, and anything beyond the last eight drops off a cliff — 1.7% for a semi-final, 0.08% to lift the trophy. A grind-it-out campaign with a real but narrow knockout window.

Australia.text:
Australia arrive ranked 27th in the world with a modestly valued squad at €77.45m, and a recent record that pulls in two directions. The Socceroos closed their FIFA Series in March with real authority — a 1-0 win over Cameroon and a 5-1 demolition of Curaçao — but the wider picture is patchier, with four defeats in their last ten, including limp scorelines away to Colombia (0-3), Venezuela (0-1) and Mexico (0-1). The most recent outing, a 1-1 draw in Switzerland, reads as a respectable benchmark against stronger opposition.

The model treats them as a credible but not dangerous knockout side. It gives Australia a 68.8% chance of escaping the group stage at the round-of-32 cut, but only a 33.6% shot at reaching the last 16 and an 11.5% chance of a quarter-final. Winning the group is rated at 21%, while the deep runs thin out fast — 3.7% to a semi-final and just 0.3% to lift the trophy. In short, the numbers frame a team likely to feature into the second week, with little expectation beyond it.

Saudi Arabia.text:
Saudi Arabia arrive at this World Cup ranked 61st in the world and carrying one of the lighter squads in the field, valued at just €40.68m. The recent form does little to inspire: the 3-0 friendly win over Puerto Rico in June was a welcome lift, but it followed back-to-back defeats to Ecuador and Serbia, a 0-4 home thrashing by Egypt, and a patchy Arab Cup that ended with losses to Morocco and Jordan. The defence has leaked freely, and with no listed international goals among the named players, the goal threat looks an open question.

The model is unsentimental about it. It gives the Green Falcons a 30.7% chance of escaping the group into the round of 32, but only a 1.3% shot at winning their group outright. Beyond that the road narrows sharply: 4.1% to reach the last 16, 0.8% to the quarter-finals, and effectively no path to the title. This is a squad the numbers frame as an outsider hoping to spring a single result rather than build a run, and the recent results give little reason to argue the model is being harsh.

Uzbekistan.text:
Uzbekistan arrive ranked 50th in the world and one of the lighter squads in the field, with a market value of just €85.3m, and the model treats them accordingly. It gives them a 43.9% chance of surviving the group into the round of 32 — close to a coin flip — but only 14.2% to reach the last 16 and 6.2% to actually win their group. Beyond that the numbers fall away fast: 3.9% to make a quarter-final, and a token 0.05% to lift the trophy. This is a side the model expects to be competitive for a knockout place and little more.

The recent form supports that reading without flattering it. A run through late 2025 brought wins over Kuwait, Egypt and goalless draws against Iran, but the step up in class has exposed them: back-to-back June friendly defeats to Canada (0-2) and the Netherlands (1-2) came after a flat 0-0 against Venezuela and a 3-1 over Gabon. Solid against modest opposition, stretched against better — which is roughly the story those R32 odds tell.

Jordan.text:
Jordan arrive at their second straight major tournament ranked 63rd in the world, with one of the leaner squads in the field at just €20.3m. The model sees Al Nashama as long shots to advance: a 14.1% chance of reaching the round of 32, 1.6% to make the round of 16, and effectively nothing beyond the quarter-finals, where the line sits at 0.3%. Winning their group is priced at barely half a percent. None of that is harsh given the gulf in resources, but it does frame this as a campaign about survival rather than progress.

The form line tells two stories. Through the 2025 Arab Cup, Jordan looked genuinely dangerous, winning five in a row including a 3-0 at Egypt and a 1-0 at Saudi Arabia before falling 3-2 to Morocco. Since then the warm-up results have cooled the optimism: two friendly draws against Costa Rica and Nigeria, then defeats by 1-4 to Switzerland and 0-2 to Colombia. The defence that shut out three Arab Cup opponents conceded six across those two losses, and that's the question they carry into the group.

Qatar.text:
Qatar arrive at the World Cup ranked 55th and carrying one of the leanest squads in the field, valued at just €19.93m, and recent form does little to lift the mood. The Maroons have managed only one win in their last ten, a 2-1 home result over the United Arab Emirates in qualifying back in October 2025. Since then the picture has darkened: a winless Arab Cup featuring a 0-3 home defeat to Tunisia and losses to Palestine, a 1-2 reverse at home to Zimbabwe, and goalless draws with Oman and El Salvador either side of a narrow loss to the Republic of Ireland.

The model reads all of this plainly. It gives Qatar a 23.3% chance of surviving the group into the round of 32, but only 2.9% of reaching the round of 16 and a vanishing 0.2% of making the quarter-finals. Winning the group sits at 1.1%, and the title odds are effectively zero. On these numbers, simply progressing past the first stage would count as a strong tournament for a side struggling badly to score.

New Zealand.text:
New Zealand arrive as one of the tournament's makeweights, ranked 85th in the world with a squad valued at just €34.35m, and the form line does little to lift the mood. The last ten games yielded a single win — a 4-1 demolition of Chile in March — alongside a lone draw against Norway and eight defeats, including a 0-4 thrashing by Haiti and a 0-1 loss to England in the most recent friendlies. Back-to-back losses to Australia bookend a run that reads as a team comfortable against weaker opposition but routinely outclassed above its level.

The model sees roughly that. It gives New Zealand a 40.8% chance of surviving the group into the round of 32, but the odds thin sharply after that: 10.8% to reach the last 16, under 2% to make a quarter-final, and effectively zero to win the thing. Winning the group is a 6.4% long shot. With three goalkeepers and five defenders among the named men — Tyler Bindon and Michael Boxall anchoring the back line — this looks like a side built to stay compact and hope to nick a result rather than chase one.

Norway.text:
Norway arrive ranked 31st in the world but carrying a squad valued at €589.9m, and the qualifying campaign suggests that price tag is earned rather than inflated. The European route was emphatic: an 11-1 demolition of Moldova, a 4-1 win away to Italy, a 5-0 dismissal of Israel and a 4-1 result against Estonia all point to a side that scores in volume when the gap in quality is real. The friendly form is harder to read — a draw in Morocco, a goalless stalemate with Switzerland and a 1-2 loss in the Netherlands sit alongside a confident 3-1 over Sweden — so the picture is of a team that punishes weaker opponents but hasn't yet proven it against the genuine heavyweights.

The model reflects that ambivalence. It makes Norway 81.5% to clear the round of 32 and gives them a 43.7% shot at the last 16, but the line steepens fast after that: 19% to reach the quarters, 7.8% to the semis and just 1.05% to lift the trophy. Winning the group is a coin-toss-and-a-half at 20.5%. A capable side, not a favourite.

Sweden.text:
Sweden arrive ranked 38th in the world with a squad worth €406m, but the form line reads like a warning. Their World Cup qualifying campaign was grim — beaten by Kosovo home and away, thrashed 4-1 and 2-0 by Switzerland, and held by Slovenia twice — before late wins over Ukraine and Poland steadied things. The recent friendlies offered little comfort either: a 1-3 loss to Norway and a 2-2 draw with Greece. This is a side built around defenders, with Lindelöf, Hien, Lagerbielke and Ekdal anchoring a backline that has too often leaked goals.

The model is unconvinced and the numbers explain why. It gives Sweden just a 49.9% chance of clearing the group stage — essentially a coin flip — and only 8.3% to win their group. Beyond that the path narrows sharply: 12.7% to reach the last 16, 4% to the quarter-finals, and a barely-there 0.06% to lift the trophy. For a nation with this defensive pedigree the floor should be solid, but on recent evidence even surviving the group is a genuinely open question rather than a formality.

Czech Republic.text:
The Czech Republic arrive ranked 41st with a squad valued at €188.18m, and the model frames them as a side likely to make the tournament's main draw but no further. It gives them a 60.9% chance of reaching the round of 32, but only 19.5% to make the round of 16 and 4.2% to reach the quarter-finals; winning the group sits at 11.8%, and anything deeper than that is a long shot, with the semi-finals at 0.8% and the title essentially off the table at 0.02%.

Recent form reads steadily rather than spectacularly. Friendly wins over Guatemala (3-1) and Kosovo (2-1) followed competitive qualifying outings, including a 1-1 with Denmark, a 2-2 against the Republic of Ireland and a goalless draw with Croatia, while a 6-0 thrashing of Gibraltar flattered the attack. The blemish is a 1-2 defeat away to the Faroe Islands in October, a result that hints at the inconsistency the model is pricing in. With three goalkeepers and a defence-heavy named group, the Czechs look built to grind out results rather than overwhelm anyone.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.text:
Bosnia and Herzegovina arrive ranked 65th in the world with a squad valued at €151.6m, and the model treats them as long shots once the bracket opens up. It gives them just a 40.4% chance of clearing the round of 32, a 7.1% shot at the round of 16, and effectively nothing beyond — 0.9% to reach the quarter-finals and a rounded zero for the title. Winning the group is priced at 2.5%, so survival rather than seeding is the realistic ceiling here.

The recent form is steadier than the ranking suggests. Across their last ten they avoided defeat in nine, the only loss a 1-2 at home to Austria back in September 2025, and they showed teeth in qualifying with a 3-1 win over Romania, a 4-1 at Malta and a 6-0 at San Marino. The warm-up draws against Panama and FYR Macedonia were flatter, and the squad in front of goalkeepers Vasilj and Jurkas leans heavily on experienced defenders like Kolasinac and Katic. That profile fits the numbers: hard to beat, but the model sees little scope to go deep.

Algeria.text:
Algeria arrive in good order. A 1-0 win away to the Netherlands in June is the kind of result that travels, and it sits alongside a goalless draw with Uruguay and a 7-0 demolition of Guatemala in a friendly run that suggests the attack is sharp and the defence resilient. The Africa Cup of Nations told a more mixed story — three wins, including 3-0 over Sudan, before a 2-0 loss to Nigeria — but ranked 28th in the world with a squad valued at €256.9m, this is a side built around established names like Aït-Nouri and Bensebaïni.

The model treats them as solid rather than spectacular. Reaching the round of 32 is close to a formality at 84.6%, but it has them as only marginal favourites to win their group at 15.5%, and the survival curve steepens quickly thereafter: 30.9% to make the last 16, 15.2% to reach the quarter-finals, and just 6.4% to go further. A title shout sits at 0.7%. The realistic ambition here is a knockout berth, with anything beyond the last 16 counting as genuine overachievement.

Ghana.text:
Ghana arrive 74th in the world and carrying a split personality. The qualifying campaign that booked their ticket was tidy and ruthless — wins over Comoros, Mali and a 5-0 dismantling of the Central African Republic, with only a draw in Chad blotting the run. But the friendlies since have been grim viewing: a 1-5 thrashing in Austria, a 1-2 loss to Germany, defeats to Japan, South Korea and Mexico, and most recently a 1-1 draw in Wales. For a squad valued at €234.6m, that is a worrying gap between competitive intensity and exhibition form.

The model reads them as a side that should escape the group stage in the expanded format but go no further with any regularity. It gives Ghana a 47.5% chance of reaching the round of 32 — essentially a coin flip — but only 9.7% to make the last 16 and 2% to reach a quarter-final. Winning the group is a 3.8% long shot, and the championship sits at 0.01%, which is to say it isn't happening. This is a team built to make up the numbers, not the latter rounds.

Cape Verde.text:
Cape Verde arrive at their first World Cup as a side that earned the trip the hard way, ranked 69th in the world and worth a modest €54.5m. The qualifying run did the heavy lifting: a 1-0 home win over Cameroon, a 2-0 victory in Mauritius and a 3-0 dismantling of Eswatini, with only a 3-3 draw in Libya blotting the campaign. The warm-up form has been encouraging too — back-to-back 3-0 friendly wins over Serbia and Bermuda, and a 1-1 draw with Finland — though a 4-2 defeat in Chile is a reminder of the step up in class.

The model is blunt about where that leaves the Tubarões Azuis. It gives them a 31% chance of surviving the group stage into the round of 32, but only 4.2% of reaching the last 16 and 0.9% of a quarter-final. Winning the group is priced at just 1.4%, and the title at effectively zero. In short, this is a tournament about the experience and the occasion; clearing one knockout hurdle would already count as a genuine overachievement for a debutant nation.

Curaçao.text:
The numbers that matter for Curaçao start with how they got here. Their CONCACAF qualifying run was unbeaten across the stretch in our records: a 7-0 demolition of Bermuda, a 2-0 home win over Jamaica, plus draws away to Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago that did the quiet work. Ranked 82nd in the world with a squad valued at €25.78m — modest by tournament standards — this is a side built on organisation rather than star power, with three goalkeepers and a defensive spine led by Bazoer and Brenet headlining the named group.

The friendlies since tell a harder story. Heavy defeats away to Australia (1-5), China (0-2) and Scotland (1-4) suggest the step up against ranked opposition is steep, even after a 4-0 send-off against Aruba. The model reads it cautiously: just an 8.1% chance of reaching the round of 32, 0.83% to make the last 16, and barely 0.49% to win the group. Simply being here is the achievement; the simulations treat anything beyond the group stage as a long shot worth watching rather than backing.

Haiti.text:
Ranked 83rd in the world and carrying a squad valued at just €55.9m, Haiti arrive at the World Cup as one of CONCACAF's longer shots, and the model treats them that way. It gives them a 24.9% chance of surviving the group stage into the round of 32, but only a 4.96% chance of reaching the round of 16 and under 1% of going further. Winning their group is priced as a 1.27% event. The path here was earned the hard way: qualification ran through draws with Honduras and Costa Rica, a 3-0 win in Nicaragua, and home victories over Costa Rica and Nicaragua to close out the campaign.

The warm-up results were a mixed bag worth weighing. A 4-0 thumping of New Zealand showed the ceiling, but defeats to Peru (1-2) and Tunisia (0-1) and a 1-1 draw with Iceland point to a side that can be contained. With a defence built around Ade, Delcroix and Duverne and three goalkeepers competing for the gloves, Haiti's hopes rest on tight, low-scoring games rather than outscoring better-resourced opponents.

Iraq.text:
Iraq arrive at the World Cup having earned their place the hard way, edging Bolivia 2-1 in the intercontinental play-offs in April before a confidence-building friendly run that included a 1-0 win over Andorra and a creditable 1-1 draw away to Spain in June. Ranked 57th in the world and carrying one of the leaner squads in the field at just €21.2m, the Lions of Mesopotamia look set up to defend first: that goalless draw away to Saudi Arabia and a 0-0-flavoured cluster of tight Asian qualifiers point to a side that lives on fine margins rather than firepower.

The model is blunt about the ceiling. It gives Iraq a 13.6% chance of surviving the group into the round of 32, but only 2.3% to reach the round of 16 and effectively nothing beyond — a 0.3% semi-final shot rounds the story off. Winning the group is priced at under 1%. The recent Arab Cup, where back-to-back losses to Algeria and Jordan followed a bright start, captures the issue plainly: Iraq can compete with anyone for a half, but stringing together knockout-level performances is another matter entirely.

H. Kane.text:
Kane arrives at this tournament on the steepest upward curve of his Bayern spell. His debut German season was hardly quiet — 26 league goals in 31 games at a 7.7 rating — yet 2025 was simply better, 36 Bundesliga goals from the same 31 appearances, plus 14 in 13 Champions League ties and 10 in six cup matches at an 8.05 rating. The finishing isn't tailing off at 32; if anything it's accelerating, and his ratings now sit comfortably around the 7.9-8.0 mark across competitions.

For England the pattern holds. He scored eight goals in eight World Cup qualifiers across the 2024 campaign, then opened the latest cycle with two in two qualifiers (8.1 rating) and another in a friendly. That's a striker converting at a rate his whole career suggests he can sustain into a major tournament. With England ranked fourth in the world, Kane is the model's clearest individual reason to take their goal output seriously — a scorer in the form of his life.

J. David.text:
The shape of David's last two club seasons is a story of a step up that hasn't yet paid off. At Lille in 2024 he was prolific and trusted, 16 Ligue 1 goals across 32 games at a 7.15 rating, with nine more in the Champions League. The Juventus move flattened that: six Serie A goals from 35 appearances but only 1,801 minutes, a rating down to 6.43, and a thin two goals at a 6.3 rating in Europe. That's a player rotated more and scoring less in a tougher system.

The encouraging counterweight is his Canada record, which has stayed sharp regardless of his club mood — 7.21 across 2025 friendlies and two goals in four outings at 7.23 already in 2026. For a side ranked 30th, that gap matters: the national-team David still looks like the focal point Lille had, not the muted version Turin has seen. Expect his tournament output to track the Canada line rather than the Serie A one.

Mikel Oyarzabal.text:
Oyarzabal's club output is trending the right way at exactly the right time. His La Liga numbers jumped from nine goals in 2,262 minutes across 2024 to 15 in 2,714 minutes through 2025, with his league rating climbing from 6.79 to 7.08 — a striker scoring more often and contributing more across the board. The cup work backs it up: four goals and four assists in just four 2024 Copa del Rey ties at an 8.28 rating shows he sharpens in knockout football, the format that decides a World Cup.

For Spain, the case is even stronger. He hit six goals and four assists in six European qualifiers at 7.88, then opened 2026 with two goals in two friendlies off 63 minutes and an 8.7 rating. That is a player finishing chances at a rate well above his career baseline. Behind a top-ranked side, the 28-year-old projects as a reliable scorer rather than a peripheral squad option — a genuine asset for a deep run.

Kylian Mbappé.text:
Mbappé's two seasons at Real Madrid leave little doubt about the floor of his output: 31 La Liga goals in 34 appearances across 2024, then 25 in 31 in 2025, with a Champions League haul that jumped from 7 in 14 games to a startling 15 in just 11. That European return, at an 8.05 rating, is the form of a player who scores in the matches that matter most — exactly the profile a tournament rewards. For France, the qualifying campaign was the standout: 5 goals and 3 assists in 4 games at an 8.38 rating, the best number on his page.

The one caution is recent. His 2026 friendlies show a single goal in 4 outings and a 219-minute load, with the rating dipping to 7.03 — sharp enough, but short of the club ceiling. Backed by the world's top-ranked side, he arrives as a genuine Golden Boot contender; the friendly lull is the only reason to wait for the group stage before taking that as read.

Lautaro Martínez.text:
The numbers here describe a goalkeeper, and a busy one: across 2024 he started a full Premier League season for Aston Villa, 37 appearances and 3,196 minutes at a 7.09 rating, with his sharpest work coming in the Champions League, where 12 games returned a 7.42. The trend since then is gently downward. The 2025 league campaign brought 32 appearances at 6.98, lifted slightly by an 11-game Europa League run rated 7.12, and his single assist of the period. Into 2026, sixteen World Cup qualifiers for Argentina produced a 6.93 rating over 1,459 minutes.

That points to a steady, well-used keeper rather than one peaking into the tournament — the ratings have slipped from 7.09 to 6.98 to 6.93 across the three windows. For a side ranked third in the world, that is dependable form holding around a 6.9-7.0 baseline, but the modest dip in the qualifiers is worth watching rather than dismissing.

E. Haaland.text: Haaland's club output has stayed remarkably level: 22 Premier League goals in 32 appearances across 2024, then a career-best 27 in 35 with eight assists in 2025, his rating ticking up from 7.25 to 7.31. The Champions League returns mirror that ceiling — eight goals in ten games in each season — so this is a striker who scores at the same elite rate whatever the stage. The bigger story for the tournament sits with Norway. He buried 16 goals in just eight World Cup qualifying matches in 2024 at an 8.25 rating, and seven more in six Nations League outings, numbers that dwarf even his City scoring. The 2026 sample is thinner — two goals in two qualifiers, then a quiet two friendlies at a 6.50 rating — but that's noise against the body of work. At 25 and arriving in form, he is exactly the kind of finisher who can drag a 31st-ranked side deeper than its rating suggests.

Cristiano Ronaldo.text:
At 40, Cristiano Ronaldo is still converting at a rate few forwards of any age match. His Saudi Pro League returns have actually climbed, from 25 goals in 30 appearances across 2024 to 28 in 30 the following season, with another 14 in 16 King's Cup outings underlining how reliably he finishes when chances arrive. The caveat is in the surrounding numbers: his Pro League rating slipped from 7.53 to 7.16 even as the goals rose, hinting at a game increasingly narrowed to the penalty box rather than built on all-round influence.

For Portugal, the signs stay encouraging — eight goals in eight Nations League games and five in five World Cup qualifiers show the finishing translates to international level. But a single 45-minute friendly in 2026, rated 6.5, is a thin recent sample. With a fifth-ranked side around him, he remains a genuine goal threat; the open question is how much tournament football those legs can sustain.

R. Jiménez.text:
At 34, Raúl Jiménez is leaning on his international scoring more than his club output, and the trend matters. His 2024 was the high-water mark: 12 Premier League goals from 38 games at a 7.01 rating, plus a remarkable five goals in three CONCACAF Nations League appearances at an 8.77 rating. The 2025 season tells a softer story — nine league goals from 36 games and the rating slipping to 6.68, with his Mexico friendly form down to 6.77. Early 2026 friendlies have brought one goal in three at a modest 6.90.

The implication for the tournament is that Jiménez remains a credible focal point but a fading one in raw production. The international numbers flatter him against CONCACAF opposition, and his Premier League scoring has dropped a quarter year-on-year. For a model, that argues for treating him as a useful but no longer prolific finisher, capable of punishing weaker defences while unlikely to carry Mexico's attack outright at a World Cup.

L. Messi.text:
At 38, Lionel Messi's output is still climbing rather than fading. His MLS goal return has risen across three seasons — 21 in 22 appearances in 2024, a remarkable 35 goals and 23 assists in 31 games in 2025, and already 13 goals and seven assists from 14 matches in 2026, with his average rating ticking up each year from 8.33 to 8.60 to 8.67. Notably, Inter Miami now list him as a midfielder, suggesting a deeper role that hasn't dented his numbers.

The international evidence matters more for the tournament, and it's just as strong: eight goals and three assists in 12 World Cup qualifiers for an Argentina side ranked third in the world, at an 8.03 rating. The caveat is workload management — his 2026 Argentina friendlies total just 35 minutes across three caps. The form is undeniable; the open question is whether 38-year-old legs are being rationed for the summer, and on this evidence Argentina look right to manage them.

Brahim Díaz.text:
Díaz's club trajectory has drifted in one clear direction: less central, more supporting. His 2024 La Liga return of four goals and two assists across 1,405 minutes carried a 6.86 rating, but by 2025 the goal tap closed almost entirely — one goal, though six assists, in 1,284 minutes, with the rating easing to 6.68 and the Champions League following the same dip to 6.79. At Real Madrid he is a rotation creator more than a scorer, and that matters for how heavily Morocco can lean on him.

The international picture flips the story. Pushed forward to attacker, Díaz buried seven goals in four AFCON qualifiers (an 8.22 rating) and added five at the finals proper. That is a player liberated by a freer role and a side built around him. The honest read for the tournament: his club numbers counsel caution on volume, but Morocco — ranked eighth — clearly unlock a sharper, goal-hungrier version, and his early 2026 friendlies already show one goal in four.

M. Olise.text:
Olise arrived at Bayern and produced immediately: 12 goals and 15 assists across 34 Bundesliga games in 2024 at a 7.92 rating, with another five goals in the Champions League. The 2025 campaign was a clear step up rather than a regression — 15 goals and 19 assists in 32 league outings, plus five goals and six assists in Europe at 7.52. That's a 24-year-old midfielder pushing past 30 league goal involvements in a full season, with the underlying rating barely moving. The consistency across two years, in a top side and a deep Champions League run, is the kind of profile that travels well into a tournament.

For France, top of the FIFA ranking, the early signs are loud: three goals and an assist in just 234 friendly minutes in 2026, plus two goals in five World Cup qualifiers at an 8.42 rating in 2024. Everything in the record points to a creator entering the tournament at peak output rather than hoping to find it.

F. Wirtz.text:
Wirtz arrives in different shape than the prodigy who tore up the Bundesliga. In his final 2024 Leverkusen campaign he posted 10 goals and 12 assists across 31 league games at a 7.70 rating, with another six goals in the Champions League. The 2025 move to Liverpool flattened that output: 33 Premier League appearances yielded just five goals and three assists, and his rating slid to 6.81 — a clear step down from the numbers that made his name. The Champions League work was steadier at 7.19, but the headline drop is real and worth weighing against the hype.

What tips the read back toward optimism is the Germany shirt. In four 2026 friendlies he has already produced three goals and two assists at a 7.95 rating, easily his sharpest recent form. At 22 he remains central to Germany's attack, and the international setting has consistently lifted him above his club ceiling — the most encouraging signal heading into the tournament.

B. Embolo.text:
Embolo's club output has quietly climbed. His final Ligue 1 season at Monaco brought 6 goals and 4 assists across 29 games at a 6.75 rating; the move to Rennes lifted that to 9 goals and 3 assists in 31 appearances, even if the underlying rating barely moved at 6.71. So the headline goals are up while the all-round numbers hold steady — a striker doing his core job a little better, not transforming his game.

What should reassure Switzerland is the gap between his club and country form. The same player who rates in the high 6s in France posted a 7.23 across World Cup qualifying, scoring 4 in 6, then carried that into 3 friendly goals in 2025 and 2 more in 2026 at a 7.27 clip. That's a meaningful pattern: Embolo reliably produces more for the national side than his league baseline suggests. For a 28-year-old leading the line of a 19th-ranked team, the implication is a forward arriving in form and historically sharper in this exact shirt.

V. Gyökeres.text:
At Sporting CP in 2024 Gyökeres was a genuine phenomenon: 39 goals in 33 Primeira Liga matches at a 7.99 rating, with six more in the Champions League and a remarkable nine in six Nations League games for Sweden, where his rating hit 8.65. That is the profile of an elite penalty-box finisher.

The 2025 move to Arsenal tells a cooler story. Fourteen Premier League goals in 36 appearances is respectable output, but the rating slipped to 6.62, and his Champions League work (five in 13, rating 6.75) sat in the same modest band. The volume of chances and the easy dominance of Portugal did not fully translate to England.

For the tournament, that split matters. The model should lean on his international scoring, which has stayed strong regardless of club setting, while recognising that his year against top defences was solid rather than spectacular. With Sweden ranked 38th, Gyökeres is the swing factor: their ceiling rises or falls largely on which version turns up.

L. Díaz.text:
Díaz arrives in form that has only sharpened with each move. His last full Premier League season at Liverpool returned 13 goals and five assists across 36 games at a 7.27 rating — productive, if not prolific. The switch to Bayern unlocked something else: 15 goals and 14 assists in 32 Bundesliga matches in 2025, plus seven goals and three assists in the Champions League at a standout 7.52 rating. That is no longer a winger who chips in but a primary creator and finisher, and the assist numbers matter most for a Colombia side leaning on him.

The international evidence backs it up. Across 17 World Cup qualifiers he scored seven and set up three at a 7.25 rating, carrying real load through a CONMEBOL campaign. For a team ranked 13th, that consistency across club and country is the case for Díaz as Colombia's tournament fulcrum — a player delivering goals and chances at the same level wherever he plays.

S. Mané.text:
At 33, Sadio Mané is still producing, even if the raw output is gently sliding. His 2024 Pro League season was his peak in Saudi Arabia — 14 goals and 11 assists in 32 games at a 7.56 rating — and 2025 settled a notch lower, 10 goals and six assists across 25 league appearances with the rating easing to 7.28. The telling shift is positional: Al-Nassr increasingly used him as a midfielder rather than a pure attacker last term, which dilutes the goal numbers but keeps him heavily involved in creation.

For the tournament, the signs are encouraging. At the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations he chipped in two goals and three assists across seven games at 7.31, comfortable in that deeper role, and his lone 2026 friendly brought two goals and an 8.9 rating in 60 minutes. Senegal sit 14th in the FIFA ranking, and Mané remains their reference point in the final third — less of a guaranteed 14-goal threat now, more a creator who still finds the net when sharp.

Raphinha.text:
Raphinha arrives at the World Cup off a two-season arc that points up then gently down. The 2024 campaign was the peak: 18 goals and nine assists in La Liga at a 7.8 rating, and a barely believable 13 goals and eight assists across 14 Champions League games at an 8.25 rating. The 2025 numbers cool from there — 13 La Liga goals but only three assists and a 7.55 rating, with the Champions League output dropping to three goals and a 7.31. The move to a midfield role hasn't dimmed his scoring, and that matters for Brazil, who he's served with five goals in 13 World Cup qualifiers at 7.42.

The one flag is national-team friendlies, where he's mustered no goals and ratings of 6.6 and 6.7. So the club ceiling is genuinely elite and the qualifying form holds up; the question is whether the Brazil version arrives closer to the Barcelona one or the flat friendly form.

Vinícius Júnior.text:
At club level Vinícius keeps trending up. His 2024 La Liga return of 11 goals and 8 assists across 30 games at a 7.37 rating gave way to 16 goals in 36 in 2025, with a sharper 7.51 mark, and he was even deadlier in Europe — eight Champions League goals in just 12 outings in 2024 (a 7.56 rating) before a more creative five-and-five season after.

The caveat sits with the national team. In World Cup qualifying he managed only two goals and one assist in 11 appearances at a 6.93 rating, often shifted into midfield rather than let loose on the left. That gap between a 7.5-rated Madrid forward and a 6.9-rated Brazil one is the open question heading into the tournament. The Real Madrid version is among the most dangerous attackers on the planet; the Brazil version has been quieter and positioned further from goal. Which one shows up will go a long way to deciding how far the sixth-ranked side runs.

K. De Bruyne.text:
The headline number with De Bruyne is the move and what it has and hasn't cost him. His final Manchester City Premier League season in 2024 brought 4 goals and 7 assists across 33 games at a 7.32 rating, solid creative output if a step down from his peak. The 2025 switch to Napoli has, if anything, sharpened his goalscoring: 5 goals in 18 Serie A appearances, though the assist count has thinned to 2 and the rating dipped slightly to 7.04. At 34, that profile reads as a still-productive operator rather than a dominant one.

For the tournament, the more compelling evidence sits in a Belgium shirt. His World Cup qualifying return of 6 goals and 1 assist in 6 games at an 8.27 rating is exceptional, and a 7.33 rating across four 2026 friendlies suggests he arrives in rhythm. For a ninth-ranked side, De Bruyne remains the creative pivot the model leans on.

Son Heung-Min.text:
Son's recent club arc reads like a player reinventing himself. His final Tottenham season was steady rather than spectacular — seven goals and nine assists across 30 Premier League games at a 7.26 rating — before the move to Los Angeles FC sparked him: 12 goals in just 11 MLS appearances in 2025, an outlier 8.18 rating that flattered to deceive. Because 2026 tells a different story. In 13 MLS league games this year he has scored zero, though he has piled up eight assists; in the CONCACAF Champions League it's two goals and six assists. At 33, the finisher is morphing into a creator at club level.

That matters less than it looks, because for South Korea he remains lethal. Seven goals and four assists in 13 World Cup qualifiers, a 7.81 rating, says the international version is still scoring freely. For a side ranked 25th, that gap between dry club goalscoring and sharp national-team output is the key read: expect Son to create as much as he converts in 2026.

Bruno Fernandes.text:
Bruno Fernandes arrives at this tournament as a metronome of consistency rather than a fading 31-year-old. His Premier League output has actually trended upward: 8 goals and 10 assists across 3,024 minutes in 2024, then 9 goals and a striking 21 assists in 2025, the rating barely moving from 7.61 to 7.63. That assist jump matters most for Portugal — it signals a player creating more for others even as United struggled around him, and his knack for stepping up in cup football (8.05 in the Europa League, 7 goals, plus 8.4 in the League Cup) suggests the big stage suits him.

His early-2026 friendly form is modest by his standards (7.5, one goal and one assist in 214 minutes), but that's a small sample. For a Portugal side ranked fifth in the world, the implication is clear: Fernandes remains a reliable engine of chances, and on volume of assists alone he is among the more dependable creative bets in the field.

S. Rahimi.text:
Rahimi's club output tells a story of cooling form. The 2024 season was his peak at Al Ain: eight goals in 18 Pro League games at a 7.44 rating, plus a ruthless five in seven AFC Champions League Elite outings (7.54). That version of him was among the most productive attackers in the UAE.

The 2025 picture is leaner. Just two Pro League goals across 15 appearances and a sub-7 rating (6.98), then a blank in three Club World Cup games at 6.85. His early 2026 friendly form — one goal in 175 minutes, a 6.68 rating — points the same direction.

The caveat that matters for the tournament: Rahimi scores for Morocco even when his club numbers sag. He buried five in three Africa Cup of Nations matches and added three in five qualifiers. So the dossier reads as a striker whose club rhythm has dipped but whose international finishing has stayed sharp — a genuinely open question heading into 2026.

C. Gakpo.text:
Gakpo's club trajectory has flattened just as the tournament approaches. His 2024 Liverpool season was his sharpest: 10 Premier League goals and four assists in 35 games at a 7.22 rating, with ruthless cup returns on top (five goals in six League Cup outings). The 2025 campaign tells a quieter story — seven league goals and five assists across 36 matches, but the rating slipped to 6.89 as he was used more as a midfielder than an out-and-out attacker, and his ceiling shows: zero goals in seven FA Cup and Champions League appearances early on.

The encouraging signal is that he raises his game in orange. He was lethal in World Cup qualifying for the seventh-ranked Dutch (four goals, four assists, an 8.06 rating), and his 2026 friendly form holds up at 7.85 with two goals in four. The club dip tempers expectations, but his international record argues he turns up when it matters most.

M. Taremi.text:
Taremi's last two years tell a clear story of a player who needed minutes and found them. At Inter in 2024 he was a fringe figure, just 816 Serie A minutes across 26 appearances for a single league goal, though his Champions League numbers were healthier at a 7.08 rating with a goal and three assists in 714 minutes. The 2025 move to Olympiakos restored him: 10 goals and a 7.07 rating in 1,261 Super League minutes, plus two more in the Champions League. That rhythm has carried into international football, where his World Cup qualifying return of five goals and four assists in 15 games, at a standout 7.76 rating, is comfortably his best work in this dossier.

For the tournament, the read is encouraging. At 33 he is playing regularly and scoring, and an Iran forward delivering a near-goal-involvement-a-game in qualifying is exactly the profile you want leading the line. The Inter slump looks like a usage problem, not a decline.

A. Ueda.text:
Ueda's club trajectory points one way: up. In 2024 he managed seven Eredivisie goals from 21 appearances at a 6.83 rating, useful but unremarkable. The 2025 season was a different player entirely — 25 league goals in 31 games, 2,533 minutes and a 7.17 rating, the kind of season that turns a squad striker into a focal point. He carried that into 2026 World Cup qualifying, where he scored eight times in nine matches at a 7.49 rating, the best number on his page.

The caveat is the step up in level. Outside the Eredivisie his returns thin out — one goal in six Europa League games, blanks in limited Champions League minutes — and three recent Japan friendlies brought no goals at a 6.37 rating. So the profile is a striker in genuinely hot domestic and qualifying form whose ceiling against the tournament's best is still unproven. For a Japan side ranked 18th, that finishing run makes him a real threat; the open question is whether it travels.

Lamine Yamal.text:
At 18, Lamine Yamal's trajectory points one way: up. His 2024 La Liga return of 9 goals and 13 assists at a 7.79 rating was the work of a precocious creator; his 2025 league line — 16 goals and 11 assists across 2,268 minutes, rating up to 7.95 — is that of a finished one, with the goal output nearly doubling. The Champions League tells the same story, his 8.14 rating there in 2025 his highest in any major competition, alongside 6 goals and 4 assists in ten games. A nominal shift from attacker to midfielder hasn't dulled the numbers; if anything it has broadened them.

The caveat is small but worth flagging: his only 2026 sample is two Spain friendlies, 108 minutes, no goals or assists and a modest 7.1. That's far too little to read into. For a side ranked second in the world, a forward arriving in this kind of two-season ascent is exactly the profile that wins knockout games.

Pedri.text:
Pedri arrives as a metronome rather than a goalscorer, and the numbers say as much. His 2024 La Liga campaign was his most complete in recent memory — 36 appearances, 2,808 minutes, four goals and five assists at a 7.62 rating — and he carried that into Spain duty, where his World Cup qualifying rating spiked to a standout 8.50 across four games with two goals. The 2025 season reshaped his output: the goals dried up to two, but the creation surged to nine assists in La Liga at a near-identical 7.54 rating, marking him out as a chance-maker more than a finisher.

The caution is recent. Across three 2026 friendlies he has logged just 90 minutes total at a 7.10 rating, so his sharpness heading into the tournament is the open question rather than his quality. For the world's second-ranked side, a fit Pedri at his 2024 European-qualifying level is a genuine tournament swing factor; a half-loaded one is a more modest bet.

Vitinha.text:
At 25, Vitinha has turned into the metronome at the centre of Europe's most demanding side, and the numbers track a player still climbing. In 2024 he posted a 7.52 Ligue 1 rating with five league goals and chipped in two goals and two assists across 17 Champions League outings at 7.56. The 2025 campaign sharpened that into something more complete: a 7.58 Ligue 1 rating with seven assists, and a striking six goals from midfield in 17 Champions League games. That his output has shifted from creator to scorer at the highest club level matters, because Portugal sit fifth in the world and will lean on him to dictate tempo.

His international form backs it up — three assists in the Nations League and a 7.68 rating across six World Cup qualifiers, his best mark anywhere. For a player this consistent across Ligue 1, the Champions League and qualifying, the read into the tournament is plainly positive: reliable minutes, rising end product, no obvious dip.

Ousmane Dembélé.text:
Dembélé's 2024 campaign at Paris Saint-Germain was the high-water mark: 21 goals and seven assists in 30 Ligue 1 appearances at a 7.72 rating, plus eight goals and six assists across 15 Champions League games. That is centre-forward output from a wide attacker, and it is the form France will hope travels.

The 2025 numbers cool slightly but stay elite. Ten goals and seven assists in 22 league games (7.41) and another eight in the Champions League (7.16) confirm the goal threat is real rather than a one-season spike, even if the assist rate and overall ratings have edged down. The caveat sits in 2026: just two France friendlies, no goals, one assist, deployed in midfield at a modest 6.95. For the top-ranked side in the tournament, the open question is whether he arrives as PSG's penalty-box finisher or a deeper, less decisive role player — the club ceiling is clearly higher than the recent international sample suggests.

Rayan Cherki.text:
At 22, Cherki arrives in form that has only broadened. His final Lyon season in 2024 was the breakout — 8 goals and 11 assists across 30 Ligue 1 games at a 7.63 rating, plus 4 goals and 8 assists in the Europa League, where his 8.02 rating was the highest of any competition he played regularly. The move to Manchester City in 2025 tested whether that creativity would survive a deeper squad, and the assist count says it did: 12 in 33 Premier League appearances, even as the goals settled to 4 and the rating to 7.20. He also chipped in 3 Champions League goals.

The pattern is consistent — a provider first, a scorer second, productive in two leagues and in Europe. For France, already the model's top-ranked side, that profile reads as squad depth rather than a guaranteed starter: his 184 friendly minutes in 2026 yielded one goal and a 7.27 rating, the work of a creator still earning his place.

Jude Bellingham.text:
Bellingham's club output has drifted gently downward rather than collapsed. At Real Madrid his 2024 La Liga campaign returned nine goals and eight assists across 31 games at a 7.48 rating; in 2025 that eased to six goals and four assists in 28 league outings at 7.28, with his Champions League rating slipping from 7.45 to 7.20. Solid, productive numbers, but no longer the eye-catching debut-season surge. The early 2026 sample is tiny — two World Cup qualifiers and a friendly — yet a 7.6 qualifier rating and an assist suggest he arrives ticking over.

The more interesting signal is what England get from him. His best ratings come in a national shirt: a standout 8.33 across four Nations League games where he played as an attacker, a goal and two assists included. At 22 and central to a fourth-ranked side, he projects as a high-floor contributor rather than a guaranteed talisman — capable of decisive moments, but on current form not the runaway top scorer his 2024 hinted at.

Unai Simón.text:
Unai Simón arrives as a settled, heavily-used number one rather than a question mark. Across 2025 he was Athletic Club's workhorse, playing 37 La Liga matches for 3,330 minutes at a 6.88 rating, with another eight Champions League outings at a slightly thinner 6.50. The previous season carried more polish — a 7.09 La Liga mark and, more tellingly, a 7.22 across six Euro 2024 games for Spain, the kind of major-tournament return that travels well. The blemishes are isolated rather than structural: a 4.60 in the 2025 Super Cup stands out precisely because nothing around it does.

For a Spain side ranked second in the world, that profile reads as dependable continuity. His two 2026 friendly appearances landed at 7.30, a small but encouraging signal that he is arriving in form.
